title: In Syria, a library of Islamist texts sees light of day a decade on
gist: A 72-year-old Muslim Brotherhood sympathiser in Homs recovered a hidden library of mainly Islamist texts, walled up in 2011, found more than 90 percent intact after Assad's December 2024 fall; the story illustrates the opening of previously banned literature under Syria's new Islamist authorities amid ongoing damage and sectarian tensions.

insights.claim: Since Assad's fall, many previously banned works, including accounts of torture in Syrian prisons and radical Islamic theology, now sit openly in Syrian bookstores.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Marks a real liberalization of expression under the new order, relevant to assessing Syria's political trajectory.
insights.locator: Assad's fall saw many previously-banned works

insights.claim: A Homs resident's hidden library of mostly Islamist books, including works by Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb, walled up in 2011, was found more than 90 percent intact after he returned following Assad's December 2024 ouster.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Illustrates the depth of suppressed Islamist sympathy now able to surface in Syria.

insights.claim: Syria's new Islamist authorities, led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former jihadist, face the delicate task of reunifying a fractured country.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Reunification success is the key variable for Syria reconstruction and sanctions-relief trades.

insights.claim: Muslim Brotherhood sympathy is widespread in Syria, rooted in decades of violent suppression such as the 1982 Hama massacre, whose death toll estimates range from 10,000 to 40,000.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Brotherhood-aligned currents may gain influence in post-Assad Syria, which matters for Gulf states hostile to the Brotherhood.

insights.claim: Homs remains heavily damaged, and the religiously diverse city has seen several waves of attacks on the Alawite minority since Assad's fall.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Sectarian violence and war damage remain obstacles to Syrian stability and reconstruction investment.

insights.claim: Residents like Alwan express hope that the new government will live up to its responsibility regarding the sacrifices made in Syria, signalling expectations pressure on the new rulers.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Public expectations are high; failure to deliver could erode support for the new authorities.
insights.quote: We hope the (new) government will live up to its responsibility regarding the sacrifices made in Syria.
insights.locator: The sweetest moment of my life
